title: Quantile-Driven Mini-Buckets and Opportunistic Kernel Fallback
body:
Summary:

This note proposes a lightweight, production-friendly strategy for handling variable sequence lengths with lower padding overhead and predictable latency: quantile-driven mini-buckets combined with opportunistic kernel fallback and per-bucket KV sharding. The approach is targeted at high-throughput hosted endpoints and Dedicated pools where reducing per-token cost without impacting tail latency is critical.

Motivation and pain points:
- Large variance in sequence length (e.g., short chat turns mixed with long documents) forces large padding if using fixed-size buckets, wasting GPU cycles.
- Fine-grained bucketing reduces padding but increases scheduling overhead, kernel dispatch overhead, and KV cache fragmentation.
- Aggressive compaction can hurt tail latency when long requests miss the faster kernel or when KV locality is lost.
- Existing strategies at Redwood (time-window batching, slot compaction) work well but either keep too coarse buckets or are complex to tune per-model/workload.

Design goals:
1) Reduce average padding overhead by aligning pack sizes to observed quantiles of sequence length distribution.
2) Keep the number of bucket classes small (micro-buckets) to limit scheduling and kernel-selection complexity.
3) Provide a safe, latency-preserving fallback path: opportunistic kernel delegation to a latency-optimized but lower-throughput kernel on tail cases.
4) Preserve KV cache locality through lightweight per-bucket sharding and grace periods to avoid rewarm penalties.
5) Be incremental: can be toggled per-route and rolled out via canary.

Core idea (high level):
1) Runtime observes sequence length histogram in rolling windows (default 60s) and computes a small set of quantiles (e.g., 25th, 50th, 75th, 90th).
2) Build 3–5 mini-buckets around those quantiles (e.g., [0..q25], (q25..q50], (q50..q75], (q75..q90], (q90..inf]).
3) Each incoming request is tentatively assigned to a mini-bucket. The scheduler attempts to coalesce requests within the same mini-bucket for a short micro-window (e.g., 10–25ms) to form a pack aligned to the bucket's effective max length.
4) For each mini-bucket the runtime maintains a preferred kernel profile (fast-small-kernel vs wide-kernel vs quantized-kernel). The preferred kernel is chosen by an online cost model that mixes latency and cost per token.
5) If a bucket cannot reach enough pack density within the micro-window and the waiting request is approaching its deadline, the scheduler triggers an opportunistic kernel fallback: migrate that pack to a kernel with lower latency (possibly smaller batch-friendly kernel or single-request fast path) rather than wait or overpad.
6) KV cache is sharded by mini-bucket ID with small shared segments. Entries are tagged with the mini-bucket and have a short grace TTL on bucket transitions to avoid repeated misses during transient reassignments.

Quantile computation and windowing:
- Use exponential moving histogram quantiles computed at request arrival. The implementation must be memory-light and vectorizable (e.g., t-digest or fixed-bin linear histograms).
- Default quantiles: p25, p50, p75, p90. Configurable per-route; critical for long-tail workloads to increase p95 or p99 granularity.
- Update frequency: compute new bucket thresholds every 30–60s, with smoothing to avoid oscillation (alpha=0.2).

Mini-bucket sizing heuristics:
- Each mini-bucket gets an effective pack_max that equals its upper quantile bound or a small multiple (1.05x) to tolerate jitter.
- Limit to 3–5 buckets to keep kernel profiles manageable. For ultra-high-variance endpoints, allow adding an overflow bucket for >p95.

Kernel profile selection (online):
- Maintain per-bucket short-term stats: avg latency, p95 latency, throughput (tokens/s), GPU utilization, and unit-cost estimate.
- Candidate kernels: latency-optimized (low-latency single-threaded or specialized kernel), throughput-optimized (large-batch kernel), quantized (lower precision).
- Score each kernel for a bucket with a weighted objective: score = w_latency * SLA_score + w_cost * cost_score + w_tail * tail_score. Weights configured at route-level.
- Prefer latency kernel when p95 approaches SLA; prefer throughput/quantized when utilization is low and cost needs reduction.

Opportunistic kernel fallback (safety path):
- Trigger conditions: request wait_time >= micro-window && predicted pack_density < threshold && request_time_left < fallback_margin.
- Fallback action: schedule pack on latency-optimized kernel immediately. Optionally, mark request as "fallback_served" for metrics and QoE tracking.
- Fallback should be fast: avoid heavy reformatting between kernels; aim to share pre- and post-processing paths.

KV cache sharding and grace periods:
- Per-bucket logical shard IDs (small integer). Physical KV storage may be shared but logical tagging allows eviction policies that prefer local-bucket keys.
- When a request moves buckets (e.g., because quantiles changed), keys are not immediately evicted; apply a grace TTL (e.g., 30s) before aggressive eviction to reduce thrash.
- On fallback to latency kernel that does not use full KV cache, mark as cold-safe path: fetch missing KV eagerly with a small ahead-of-time warm-up for the next N requests in same pack if possible.

Scheduler algorithm (pseudocode):
- on_request(req):
    bucket = assign_bucket_using_quantiles(req.length)
    append_to_pending_queue(bucket, req)
    if pending_queue_size(bucket) >= desired_pack_size(bucket):
        form_pack_and_dispatch(bucket)
    else:
        schedule_timer(bucket, micro_window_ms)

- on_timer(bucket):
    pack = collect_pending_for_bucket(bucket)
    density = sum(sequence_lengths_in_pack) / (pack_size * pack_max(bucket))
    if density < density_threshold and any(req.time_left < fallback_margin):
        dispatch_pack_on_latency_kernel(pack)  // fallback
    else:
        dispatch_pack_on_preferred_kernel(pack)

Metrics and observability:
- Expose per-route and per-bucket metrics: pack_density, avg_padding_tokens, kernel_choice, fallback_rate, kv_miss_rate_by_bucket, pack_formation_latency, p95 and p99 latencies.
- Add labels for "mini_bucket_id" and "kernel_variant".
- Track cost delta relative to baseline (no bucketing) and tail latency regressions.

Testing and validation plan:
1) Synthetic workload tests: create bimodal and heavy-tail length distributions and compare padding overhead vs time-window baseline.
2) A/B canary: run on small percentage of routes with real traffic; collect cost and latency signals for 24–72 hours.
3) Stress tests: long burst workloads and KV churn scenarios to verify grace TTLs prevent rewarm storms.
4) Safety checks: enforce hard tail SLO guardrail that automatically disables quantile bucketing for a route if p99 increases by more than configured delta.

Operational knobs and configuration:
- route config options: enabled: bool, quantiles: list, micro_window_ms: int, desired_pack_multiplier: float, density_threshold: float, fallback_margin_ms: int, kv_grace_ttl_s: int, kernel_weights: map-string-to-float (expressed as tag strings in UI).
- Defaults selected to be conservative for hosted: micro_window_ms=20, desired_pack_multiplier=0.9, density_threshold=0.6, fallback_margin_ms=30, kv_grace_ttl_s=30.

Rollout plan:
- Stage 1: internal integration tests + perf bench on Dedicated dev clusters (2–3 weeks).
- Stage 2: opt-in beta for power users (selected customers) and a few internal routes (2 weeks).
- Stage 3: Canary at 1% of traffic for public hosted routes, monitor preset metrics and safety guardrails for 7 days.
- Stage 4: Gradual ramp to 20% then 100% if stable.
- Kill-switch: global feature flag per-region and per-route.

Open questions and tradeoffs:
- How often should quantiles be recomputed for bursty endpoints without causing oscillation? (we bias to slower updates and smoothing).
- Optimal number of mini-buckets vs the cost of kernel variants: empirical tuning required; propose default limit of 5.
- Interaction with multi-tenant Dedicated pools where kernel availability varies. Need to surface incompatible kernel fallback and account billing correctly.
- How to surface bucket transitions and KV shard effects to customers in Console: propose simple indicators and an "explain packing" debug trace.

Implementation notes and quick wins:
- Implement quantile estimator using fixed-bin histogram backed by atomic counters to be cheap in hot path.
- Use existing kernel abstraction layer; add a lightweight kernel hint API rather than changing dispatch surface.
- Reuse existing KV tagging metadata; add mini_bucket_id tag and grace TTL logic at eviction time.
- Instrument metrics early; fallback_rate and pack_density should be primary CI gates.

Appendix: example scenario
- Workload: 60% sequences 12–30 tokens, 30% sequences 80–140 tokens, 10% > 800 tokens.
- Quantiles: p25=18, p50=35, p75=120, p90=600. Mini-buckets: [0..18], (18..35], (35..120], (120..600], (600..inf].
- Short buckets pick latency kernel as preferred; mid buckets prefer throughput kernel; overflow bucket prefers throughput but will fall back to latency kernel for near-deadline requests to preserve SLO.
- Expected outcome: padding drops substantially for the first three buckets; a small fraction of >p90 requests hit fallback path but maintain p99 SLO.

Conclusion:
Quantile-driven mini-buckets with opportunistic kernel fallback and light KV sharding provides a pragmatic middle ground between coarse fixed buckets and heavy dynamic compaction. It reduces padding cost for common cases while offering safe, latency-preserving behavior for tails. The approach is incremental, observable, and can be tuned per-route.

Action items:
- Spike: implement quantile estimator + bucket assigner (owner: Ava Chen, 2w)
- Integrate kernel hint API and simple fallback path (owner: Diego Martinez, 3w)
- Add per-bucket metrics and canary dashboard (owner: Priya Kapoor, 1w)
- Prepare canary plan and customer opt-in doc (owner: Evan Liu, 1w)
_notes: Document created as iterative design doc for serving-runtime team; intended to be different from existing padding/coalescer RFCs by focusing on quantile-driven mini-buckets and simple KV sharding.
